en: In the waters of the ocean of the world's dissolution you held the Veda,
taking on, unwearied, the part of a ship.
Keśava, who took the body of a fish, victory, Lord of the world, Hari! (1)
The earth stands on your back, vast beyond measure,
made heaviest by the ring of scars from bearing the earth.
Keśava, who took the form of a tortoise, victory, Lord of the world, Hari! (2)
The earth dwells on the tip of your tusk, clinging there,
like the streak of the stain sunk into the moon.
Keśava, who took the form of a boar, victory, Lord of the world, Hari! (3)
On your fine lotus hand the nail is a wondrous horn
that has torn the bee that was Hiraṇyakaśipu's body.
Keśava, who took the form of the man-lion, victory, Lord of the world, Hari! (4)
With your stride you trick Bali, wondrous dwarf,
purifier of people by the water born from your toenail.
Keśava, who took the form of the dwarf, victory, Lord of the world, Hari! (5)
In water made of the blood of kṣatriyas the world, its sin removed,
you bathe, and the burning pain of existence is quenched.
Keśava, who took the form of the lord of the Bhṛgus, victory, Lord of the world, Hari! (6)
In battle you scatter to the quarters, pleasing to the guardians of the quarters,
a lovely offering of the heads of the Ten-faced one.
Keśava, who took the body of Rāma, victory, Lord of the world, Hari! (7)
On your bright body you wear a garment like a rain cloud,
the colour of the Yamunā, come together in fear of the plough's blow.
Keśava, who took the form of the plough-bearer, victory, Lord of the world, Hari! (8)
Ah! you censure the whole of the scripture's rule of sacrifice,
O compassionate heart, that shows the slaughter of animals.
Keśava, who took the body of the Buddha, victory, Lord of the world, Hari! (9)
To destroy the hordes of the mlecchas you wield a sword,
like a comet, something terrible.
Keśava, who took the body of Kalki, victory, Lord of the world, Hari! (10)
This noble song spoken by the poet Śrī Jayadeva,
hear it: it gives joy, it gives good, it is the essence of existence.
Keśava, who took forms of ten kinds, victory, Lord of the world, Hari! (11)
notes: line 6.3: the text has धृतभृघुपति (bhṛghu-, with gh), a slip for भृगुपति bhṛgupati, 'lord of the Bhṛgus', i.e. Paraśurāma. Romanized as written.

refrain: 'jaya jagadīśa hare' is 'be victorious (victory to you), Lord of the world, Hari!'; Keśava and Hari are names of Viṣṇu-Kṛṣṇa. The verse numbers of the original are kept in parentheses in en and as || n || in rom.
Romanization keeps the sandhi joins of the written text (dhṛtavānasi, nakhamadbhuta…), with spaces only where the Devanagari has them.
stanza 1: the fish (Matsya) rescues the Veda from the flood at the end of an age, acting as a boat.
line 3.2: the earth on the boar's tusk is likened to the dark mark (kalaṅka) on the moon.
line 4.2: Hiraṇyakaśipu's body likened to a bee crushed between the nails.
line 5.2: the water born from the dwarf's (Vāmana / Trivikrama's) toenail is the Ganges.

line 6.1-6.2: Paraśurāma, who destroyed the kṣatriyas, bathes the world in their blood; 'payasi' (in water) stands in the second line. The sense of the compound order is mine: 'the world, its sin removed' and 'the pain of existence quenched' both describe the world.
line 7.2: the Ten-faced one is Rāvaṇa; his heads are thrown to the ten directions as an offering (bali) to the guardians of the directions.
line 8.2: Balarāma (the plough-bearer, fair-skinned, dressed in dark blue) drags the Yamunā with his plough; the river, fearing his plough, comes to him, and her dark colour is his garment's.

line 9.1-9.2: disputed construction. darśita-paśughātam most naturally describes śrutijātam (the body of scripture 'in which the killing of animals is shown / taught'); sadayahṛdaya is then a vocative, 'O you of compassionate heart'. Some read the compound as 'with a compassionate heart that has seen (the evil of) animal slaughter'.
line 10.1: mleccha, a Sanskrit term for foreigners and outsiders to Vedic society ('barbarians'); kept untranslated.
line 10.2: kim api karālam, 'something terrible beyond words'.
